strengths: Presents a genuinely novel information-theoretic treatment of weight-only PTQ: under an iid-Gaussian weight model, the paper derives the exact rate-distortion limit via reverse waterfilling, rigorously shows that the standard entropy-coded GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large gap to this limit, and proves the proposed WaterSIC scheme is within a universal 0.255-bit gap of the IT limit for any input covariance (Theorem 3.3, with careful supporting lemmas on lattice flatness and Renyi differential-entropy convergence).

The key algorithmic idea—allocating different quantization rates (grid spacings) to different input-feature columns, mirroring classical waterfilling, combined with entropy coding rather than fixed-range scaling—is simple, well-motivated by the theory, and, to the reviewers' knowledge, not used by prior PTQ methods that apply one rate per layer or per group.

The step from the idealized 'PlainWaterSIC' to the practical 'WaterSIC' algorithm is carefully engineered with multiple well-justified refinements (LMMSE/shrinkage correction, Qronos-style activation-drift correction, residual-stream correction for down-projection layers, alternating row/column rescaler optimization, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure), each with a clear rationale grounded in the underlying loss decomposition.

Extensive empirical validation across four model families/sizes (Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-8B) and rates from 1 to 4 bits, compared against many strong and diverse baselines (GPTQ, Huffman-GPTQ/HPTQ, AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, GPTVQ, QuIP#), consistently showing improved perplexity, largely without any fine-tuning or sophisticated base quantizer/codebook, which strengthens the claim that gains stem specifically from the waterfilling-rate idea.

Thorough ablations (Figs. 7-11) isolate the contribution of each individual technique (residual correction, drift correction, attention weighting, adaptive mixing) via layerwise relative-MSE diagnostics, and additional analyses (compression rate distributions, Zstd/LZMA validation of entropy estimates, KL-divergence comparisons, zero-shot accuracy benchmarks) substantially bolster the credibility and reproducibility of the empirical claims.

The limitations section is honest and specific (no end-to-end fine-tuning integration, no hardware/throughput benchmarking of variable-length decoding, limited model scale), rather than vague or self-serving.
weaknesses: The clean 0.255-bit theoretical guarantee applies only to the idealized 'PlainWaterSIC' under an iid-Gaussian weight assumption and asymptotic (a→∞, high-rate) regime; the actual algorithm deployed in experiments ('full WaterSIC') adds many additional heuristics (drift correction, residual correction, attention weighting, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure, diagonal rescalers) that are not covered by the theoretical analysis, so the abstract's framing ('shown to be within a rate gap of 0.255 bits... uniformly over all possible covariance matrices') somewhat overstates what is proven for the method actually evaluated.

The practical pipeline has many moving parts and per-model/per-layer tuned hyperparameters (golden-section search per layer for two mixing coefficients, dead-feature threshold, damping schedules, and model-specific manual interventions such as zeroing specific outlier rows in Qwen3-8B), which raises concerns about robustness/generalization to new architectures without significant additional tuning, and about ease of reproducibility relative to simpler baselines like plain GPTQ or RTN.

Comparisons mix entropy-based and log-cardinality-based rate reporting across methods in the same plots (acknowledged by the authors), which, while transparent, complicates strictly fair comparison to codebook/lattice-based baselines (QTIP, NestQuant, QuIP#, GPTVQ, AWQ) that were not designed for variable-length entropy coding.

No benchmarking of actual inference/decoding throughput or memory overhead of the variable-length entropy-coded representation on real hardware, despite this being central to whether the reported bit-rate gains translate into practical deployment benefits; this is noted as a limitation but leaves the practical significance claims (e.g., 'new SOTA') only partially substantiated for real systems.

No fine-tuning-based baselines (e.g., PV-Tuning, AQLM, YAQA) are directly compared at matched settings, and comparisons for Llama-3-8B at the more standard 4096 context length are deferred to future work, limiting completeness of the SOTA claims relative to the strongest existing extreme-compression methods.

Single-run results without variance/error bars across evaluation metrics, making it harder to assess statistical robustness of the reported improvements, especially at very low bitrates where perplexity is highly sensitive to small changes.

strengths: Genuinely novel information-theoretic framing of layerwise weight quantization: the paper derives the exact high-rate asymptotic distortion-rate function for iid Gaussian weights, proves that standard entropy-coded GPTQ can have an arbitrarily large gap to this limit (depending on the conditioning of the Cholesky factor of Σ_X), and proves WaterSIC closes this gap to a universal 0.255 bit/dimension constant. The waterfilling connection (equalizing per-column distortion via the lattice spacing matrix A) is an elegant and, to my knowledge, new idea in the PTQ literature.
The theory (Theorem 3.3, Lemma 3.2, flatness-factor argument in Appendix B) is carried out carefully with explicit, checkable asymptotic conditions (a→∞, D→0), rather than being hand-waved.

Extensive empirical validation across four model families (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B) and a wide range of bitrates (1-4.1 bits), with consistent WikiText-2 PPL improvements over strong, recent baselines (QTIP, NestQuant, GPTVQ, QuIP#, AWQ, Huffman-GPTQ), plus zero-shot accuracy tables and KL-divergence comparisons.

Detailed engineering ablations (residual-stream correction, Qronos-style activation drift correction, attention-weighted calibration, dead-feature erasure, diagonal rescalers) are each separately diagnosed with relative-MSE plots, which aids reproducibility and understanding of where the gains come from.

The paper is unusually transparent about implementation details (hyperparameters, calibration procedure, per-layer coordinate search, outlier-row handling for Qwen3-8B) in the appendix, which is good practice for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim (0.255-bit gap to the IT limit) rests on an idealized model — iid N(0,σ²I) weight rows, independent-row optimality, and multiple asymptotic limits (n→∞, a→∞, D→0) — that does not hold for real LLM weight matrices (which are neither iid Gaussian nor are the relevant regimes high-rate/low-distortion at 1-4 bits). The paper never bridges this gap rigorously; the near-optimality guarantee is essentially a motivating heuristic for the algorithm design rather than a property verified to hold for the actual quantizers evaluated on real networks.

The practical 'full WaterSIC' algorithm (Algorithm 3-4) bundles the core waterfilling-rate idea with numerous additional, separately-motivated heuristics (LMMSE/shrinkage correction, Qronos-style activation-drift correction, residual-stream correction, two rounds of diagonal rescaler optimization, attention-weighted calibration with per-layer golden-section-search mixing, dead-feature erasure, model-specific outlier handling for Qwen3-8B). The ablations in Appendix E show several of these components (e.g., residual correction, attention weighting) contribute substantial, sometimes larger, improvements than the core per-column rate allocation. This undercuts the paper's framing that unequal/waterfilling rate allocation is 'the key innovation' driving the reported SOTA results — the empirical gains are at least as attributable to the accumulated engineering as to the IT-motivated contribution.

Rate accounting is inconsistent across compared methods: WaterSIC/Huffman-GPTQ report rates via empirical entropy while several baselines (AWQ, QTIP, GPTVQ, QuIP#, NestQuant) report rates via log-cardinality of the codebook. The paper acknowledges this but does not quantify how much of the apparent frontier improvement is simply due to entropy coding getting 'credit' for a tighter rate measure versus genuine distortion reduction at equal operational rate (i.e., equal bits actually transmitted after an optimal universal code, including convergence/overhead costs for small layers).

The claim that GPTQ can have an 'arbitrarily large gap' to the IT limit depends on the conditioning number of the per-column diagonal of L (the Cholesky factor of Σ_X); this is a worst-case statement that may not reflect typical Σ_X encountered in practice (especially with standard damping), so the practical relevance of this motivating result for real LLM layers is not empirically quantified (e.g., no reported distribution of (1/n)Σℓᵢᵢ² / Πℓᵢᵢ^(2/n) across actual layers to show the GPTQ gap is often large in practice).

No evaluation beyond 8B-parameter models; the paper explicitly defers 70B-scale evaluation, Llama-3-8B at the standard 4096 context (needed for comparison with AQLM/PV-Tuning), and comparisons against fine-tuning-based or KL/PPL-aware methods (YAQA) to future work, leaving the practical competitiveness of WaterSIC against the current state of the art for extreme compression (which typically uses fine-tuning) unaddressed.

No throughput/latency benchmarking of the entropy-coded (variable-length) representation on real hardware; given the paper's emphasis on 'new SOTA' and 'hardware support in Blackwell,' the absence of any measured decoding speed or memory-bandwidth results is a significant gap for practical significance claims.

The algorithm requires substantial per-model/per-layer tuning (golden-section search over two mixing parameters per attention layer, manual identification and zeroing of specific outlier rows in Qwen3-8B, different damping constants per model) that is not automated, raising concerns about how much manual tuning effort underlies the reported results and how well the method would generalize without such intervention to new models.

The impact statement is essentially boilerplate ('none which we feel must be specifically highlighted'), which is weak treatment of ethical/societal considerations expected of a paper proposing a new compression technology with hardware deployment implications.

strengths: Introduces a clean information-theoretic framework for weight-only linear-layer quantization, deriving a rigorous (reverse) waterfilling lower bound on achievable rate-distortion tradeoff and proving that the popular GPTQ algorithm can have an arbitrarily large gap to this limit for non-isotropic activation covariances.

Proposes WaterSIC, an algorithm with a proven (in the idealized iid-Gaussian-weight setting) 0.255-bit worst-case gap to the IT limit uniformly over all covariance matrices, backed by a careful, self-contained proof (Theorem 3.3, Lemma 3.2, flatness-factor arguments in Appendix A/B) connecting successive interference cancellation, entropy coding, and rate-distortion theory.

Strong and broad empirical validation: evaluated on four different LLMs (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B) across rates from 1 to 4 bits, consistently matching or beating a wide set of strong, diverse baselines (GPTQ/Huffman-GPTQ, AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, GPTVQ, QuIP#) in WikiText-2 perplexity, with additional KL-divergence and zero-shot accuracy comparisons.

Thorough engineering and ablation work translating the idealized algorithm into a practical one (LMMSE correction, activation-drift/Qronos correction, residual-stream correction, diagonal rescalers, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure), each individually justified and ablated with diagnostic plots (Figs. 7-11) showing where and why each component helps.

Good reproducibility: hyperparameters, binary-search/golden-section procedures, and full algorithm pseudocode (Algorithms 1-4) are provided in detail, and the authors cross-validate entropy estimates against real compressors (Zstd, LZMA) in Appendix E.
Positions the work clearly relative to a large and current body of PTQ literature, and the discussion of open questions (Pareto frontier estimates, memorization studies) adds useful context.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee (0.255-bit gap) is derived under an idealized iid N(0, σ²I) weight model with isotropic prior; real LLM weight matrices are not well described by this model (correlated, non-Gaussian, outlier-heavy), so it is unclear how much of the guarantee transfers to practice versus the many empirically-tuned heuristics added in Section 4 that lack theoretical backing.

The practical algorithm is a fairly complex composite of several heuristic corrections (drift correction, residual correction, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing with per-layer golden-section search, dead-feature erasure), which somewhat dilutes the clean 'near-optimal' narrative and raises reproducibility/complexity concerns; the computational overhead of this per-layer hyperparameter search (binary search + two golden-section searches per layer, each requiring re-quantization and forward passes) is not quantified or compared against baseline runtime.

Rate accounting is inconsistent across baselines (entropy-coded rates for WaterSIC/Huffman-GPTQ vs. log-cardinality rates for AWQ/QTIP/NestQuant/QuIP#/GPTVQ); while acknowledged, this makes some head-to-head comparisons not fully apples-to-apples, and true end-to-end compressed-model-size benchmarking against real codecs is only spot-checked on two layers (Table 6).

No experiments on larger models (e.g., 70B) or with longer context lengths matching some baselines (e.g., Llama-3-8B at 4096 context for AQLM/PV-Tuning comparison), explicitly deferred to future work, which limits confidence that gains persist at scale.

The method excludes fine-tuning/QAT by design to isolate the GPTQ-step contribution, which is reasonable for controlled comparison but means the 'new SOTA' claim should be read as SOTA among non-fine-tuned PTQ methods only, not against the overall PTQ+fine-tuning literature; this nuance could be stated more prominently in the abstract/intro rather than only implicitly.

Some reported baseline numbers (e.g., Huffman-GPTQ/GPTQ/RTN for Qwen3-8B) are taken directly from a prior paper rather than reproduced by the authors, introducing potential discrepancies in experimental conditions (calibration data, context length) that are not fully controlled for.

strengths: Novel and rigorous information-theoretic framing of linear-layer PTQ: the paper defines proper (R,D) fundamental limits for weight-only quantization under a Gaussian weight model, derives a waterfilling lower bound, and proves (Theorem 3.3, with full proofs in Appendix A/B) that standard GPTQ can have an unbounded rate gap to this limit while the proposed WaterSIC scheme is within a universal 0.255-bit gap for any input covariance matrix.

The key algorithmic idea -- allocating a different quantization step size per column proportional to 1/ℓ_ii (the Cholesky/innovation scale) rather than a single global step -- is simple, well-motivated by the AMGM argument connecting GPTQ and WaterSIC distortion formulas, and cleanly explains the empirical gains.

Extensive and carefully constructed empirical evaluation: results across five model families (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-70B) and bit rates from 1-4 bits, comparisons against a wide range of strong recent baselines (Huffman-GPTQ/HPTQ, QTIP, NestQuant, AWQ, GPTVQ, QuIP#, AQLM, PV-Tuning, YAQA), plus zero-shot downstream benchmarks and KL-divergence evaluation, consistently showing state-of-the-art or highly competitive results.

Thorough ablations and diagnostics (Appendix E-G): per-technique MSE breakdowns for residual-stream correction, drift correction, attention weighting, and adaptive mixing; empirical verification of the Gaussian-weight assumption via KS tests; verification that entropy estimates translate into real Zstd/LZMA compressed sizes; and sensitivity studies on calibration/finetuning corpus and context length.

Good reproducibility support: full algorithmic pseudocode (Algorithms 1-4), detailed hyperparameter settings, and code release; honest discussion of limitations (loss objective choice, lack of end-to-end throughput benchmarking, scale of models tested).
weaknesses: The clean theoretical guarantee (0.255-bit gap) applies only to the idealized PlainWaterSIC under iid Gaussian weight rows and asymptotic high-rate/large-a limits; the practical algorithm used in experiments (Algorithm 3) layers on many additional heuristics (LMMSE shrinkage, activation-drift correction, residual-stream correction, attention-weighted calibration with per-layer golden-section-optimized mixing coefficients, dead-feature erasure, post-hoc finetuning) that are not covered by the theory, so the strong empirical results cannot be cleanly attributed to the IT-optimality argument alone.

The Gaussianity assumption underlying the whole analysis is checked only via KS-distance goodness-of-fit on a few models (Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.2-1B) and shows non-trivial deviations for wq/wk; the paper does not analyze or bound how such deviations affect the proven 0.255-bit gap in practice.

The practical algorithm has a substantial number of hyperparameters (damping δ, dead-feature threshold τ, mixing parameters ϵ_qr/ϵ_aw optimized per layer via golden search, secant-based rate matching, LMMSE shrinkage) whose joint tuning burden and sensitivity to new architectures is not deeply analyzed, raising some concern about ease of generalization/reproducibility beyond the tested models.

Rate accounting differences between entropy-coded methods (WaterSIC, Huffman-GPTQ) and log-cardinality-based baselines (AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, QuIP#, GPTVQ) are acknowledged but could still make some cross-method comparisons not fully apples-to-apples, since entropy coding inherently captures distributional savings that fixed-rate codebooks cannot.

No end-to-end latency/throughput results are reported for the variable-length entropy-coded representation, despite this being central to practical deployment; the paper defers this to future work, which somewhat limits the practical significance claims relative to hardware-friendly fixed-rate quantizers.

strengths: First rigorous information-theoretic treatment of PTQ for linear layers: the paper derives the waterfilling lower bound (Prop 3.1), proves that standard (Huffman-)GPTQ can have an unbounded rate gap to the IT limit, and proves a clean, dimension-independent 0.255-bit gap for the proposed PlainWaterSIC/ZSIC scheme (Theorem 3.3). The connection to waterfilling, successive interference cancellation and flatness-factor arguments (Appendix A/B) is a genuinely novel and elegant framing of an otherwise purely empirical research area.

The key algorithmic insight -- setting the per-column quantization grid spacing inversely proportional to the Cholesky diagonal (i.e. to the conditional innovation variance rather than the marginal variance) -- is simple, well motivated by the theory, and is shown via ablations/entropy diagnostics (Fig. 5, Table 6) to actually produce non-uniform per-column rates in real models.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 5 models (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-70B) and a wide range of bitrates (1-4 bits), with consistent improvement over strong, recent baselines (Huffman-GPTQ/HPTQ, GPTQ, AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, QuIP#, GPTVQ, PV-Tuning, YAQA, DB-LLM, AQLM), including at the 70B scale.

Thorough engineering ablations and diagnostics (Appendix E/F/G): verification that practical codecs (Zstd/LZMA) match the predicted entropy, empirical check of the Gaussianity assumption on real weights, per-component ablations (drift correction, residual correction, attention weighting, adaptive mixing), sensitivity studies to calibration/finetuning corpus and context length, and zero-shot downstream accuracy evaluations complementing the perplexity results.
Code availability and reasonably detailed algorithmic/hyperparameter descriptions (Algorithms 1-4, Appendix D) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the theory and the deployed method: the clean 0.255-bit IT-optimality guarantee (Theorem 3.3) is proven only for PlainWaterSIC under idealized assumptions (i.i.d. Gaussian weight rows, a→∞, D→0 high-rate limit, no LMMSE/drift/residual/attention-weighting/rescaler corrections). The actual algorithm used to produce the headline SOTA results (full WaterSIC/WaterSIC-FT, Algorithm 3) includes many additional heuristics (LMMSE shrinkage, Qronos-style drift correction, residual-stream correction, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing with per-layer golden-section-tuned coefficients, dead-feature erasure, alternating row/column rescalers, and KL-based finetuning) for which no IT-optimality guarantee is given. The paper's title and framing ("information-theoretically (near) optimal") therefore somewhat overstates what is actually shown for the method that achieves the reported SOTA numbers; it is unclear how much of the empirical gain is attributable to the core waterfilling idea versus the stack of auxiliary tweaks.

The adversarial construction showing GPTQ can have an "arbitrarily large gap" to the IT limit depends on pathological covariance matrices (e.g., with very different Cholesky diagonal magnitudes); it is not established how representative such worst-case covariances are of real LLM activation statistics, somewhat undercutting the practical urgency of the gap being closed (though the empirical results do show large real-world gaps at low bitrates).

Rate accounting differences across methods (WaterSIC/Huffman-GPTQ report entropy-coded rates while several baselines such as AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, GPTVQ report log-cardinality rates) could partially confound the headline perplexity-vs-rate comparisons, since entropy coding alone (independent of the waterfilling contribution) can yield real compression gains that competitor curves do not get credit for; the paper acknowledges this but does not provide a fully rate-matched ablation isolating the waterfilling gain from the entropy-coding gain.

The practical pipeline requires numerous per-layer hyperparameters (ϵ_qr, ϵ_aw found via golden-section search per layer per rate, damping δ, secant-method rate matching, dead-feature threshold τ, etc.), raising concerns about calibration overfitting and about the method's complexity/compute cost relative to simpler baselines (no wall-clock or encoding/decoding-time comparison is provided, which is explicitly listed as a limitation).

Some baseline numbers (e.g., Qwen3-8B GPTQ/RTN/Huffman variants, Llama-3-70B RTN/QuIP/GPTQ/AWQ/PB-LLM) are taken from other papers rather than reproduced under the authors' own evaluation harness, which can introduce discrepancies in evaluation protocol (context length, calibration set, etc.) that are hard to fully control for.

Downstream zero-shot accuracy results are reported for only two of the five evaluated models (Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-8B), with the larger and more practically relevant models (Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-70B) evaluated only via perplexity, limiting the evidence that the approach's benefits generalize to task performance at larger scale.

Presentation: the paper is dense, with the complete practical algorithm, most hyperparameter details, and much of the empirical/ablation evidence relegated to a long appendix, making it difficult to assess from the main text alone how the clean theoretical story translates into the empirically evaluated method.

strengths: Provides a rigorous information-theoretic treatment of weight-only PTQ that was previously missing in the literature: derives the Gaussian rate-distortion function, proves a waterfilling converse, and shows the standard entropy-coded GPTQ algorithm can have an unbounded rate gap to the IT limit while the proposed WaterSIC is provably within 0.255 bits uniformly over all input covariances (Theorem 3.3 and surrounding analysis).

The key algorithmic idea -- per-column (in-feature) variable-rate lattice quantization derived from the Cholesky factor of the activation covariance, connected to classical waterfilling and to the Zamir-Kochman-Erez successive-refinement result -- is a genuinely novel and clean contribution that explains and fixes a real inefficiency in existing GPTQ-style algorithms (equal-rate columns via A=αI).

Extensive, carefully controlled empirical validation across five model families (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-70B) and rates from 1-4 bits, consistently matching or beating strong, diverse baselines (GPTQ, Huffman-GPTQ, AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, QuIP#, GPTVQ, PV-Tuning, DB-LLM) on perplexity, KL-divergence, and zero-shot accuracy benchmarks.

Thorough ablation studies (Appendix E) isolate the contribution of each practical refinement (LMMSE shrinkage, activation-drift/Qronos correction, residual-stream correction, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure) with relative-MSE diagnostics per layer, lending credibility to the design choices beyond aggregate perplexity numbers.

Strong reproducibility effort: full pseudocode (Algorithms 1-4), detailed hyperparameters, calibration protocols, and sensitivity analyses of calibration/finetuning corpus choice (Appendix F) are provided, along with a stated code release.

The paper explicitly checks the key modeling assumption (approximate Gaussianity of weight rows) empirically via Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests across layer types, strengthening confidence that the theory is not purely vacuous for real LLMs.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantee (0.255-bit gap) relies on an idealized i.i.d. Gaussian weight-row model and asymptotic (high-rate, large-n) limits; while the authors provide supporting KS-distance evidence, layers such as wq/wk deviate more from Gaussianity (Laplace sometimes fits better), and no finite-rate/finite-dimension bound on the gap is given to quantify how well the asymptotic result tracks the practical 1-4 bit regime used in experiments.

The final practical algorithm (Section 4) accumulates many heuristic refinements (LMMSE correction, drift correction, residual-stream correction, attention-weighted calibration with golden-section-searched mixing coefficients, dead-feature erasure, alternating row/column rescalers, post-hoc finetuning) that are not covered by the clean 0.255-bit theoretical guarantee; it is therefore unclear how much of the reported SOTA gains stem from the theoretically motivated unequal-rate idea versus from this substantial engineering stack, making the paper's core claim (near-IT-optimality) harder to disentangle from its empirical performance claims.

Some baseline numbers (e.g., Huffman-GPTQ/GPTQ/RTN for Qwen3-8B) are taken directly from a concurrent paper rather than reproduced under the authors' own evaluation harness, which introduces a risk of protocol mismatches (e.g., differing calibration data, context length, or damping) that could affect the fairness of cross-method comparisons.

The theoretical analysis treats each linear layer independently (row-wise independence assumption and layerwise MSE objective), and the cross-layer correction mechanisms (activation drift, residual stream) are heuristic fixes rather than being derived from or covered by the stated IT framework, so the paper's title claim of "information-theoretically (near) optimal" quantization applies more narrowly than the full deployed pipeline.

No end-to-end hardware/throughput benchmarking of the entropy-coding-based compressed format is provided (acknowledged as a limitation by the authors), leaving open whether the theoretical rate gains translate into practical latency/memory benefits on real inference hardware.

The dependence of final quality on calibration/finetuning corpus choice (Appendix F) shows non-trivial generalization gaps (e.g., large C4 perplexity gap when calibrating/finetuning only on WikiText-2), suggesting some fragility in the practical pipeline that is not fully explored beyond a few corpora and context lengths.
